research_branches.name: Husbandry & Agriculture
research_branches.desc: Fields, seed and livestock: the raw crops and herds of the colonies.

research_branches.name: Forestry & Mining
research_branches.desc: Timber, furs, ore and silver: the wealth of the woods and hills.

research_branches.name: Navigation & Shipbuilding
research_branches.desc: Faster hulls, better charts and fuller holds on the sea routes.

research_branches.name: Roads & the Frontier
research_branches.desc: Wagons, roads, rivers and surveyors: the land routes west.

research_branches.name: Manufacture
research_branches.desc: Mills, looms and forges: faster and thriftier workshops.

research_branches.name: Commerce & Statecraft
research_branches.desc: Markets, credit and assemblies: prices, costs and Liberty.

research.name: Crop Rotation
research.hook: Charles 'Turnip' Townshend retired to Norfolk in 1730 and championed a four-field rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover.
research.desc: Grain, tobacco, cotton and sugar cane production x2

research.name: Improved Husbandry
research.hook: Jethro Tull's book Horse-Hoeing Husbandry (1731) urged farmers to till between drilled rows; it was argued over for decades.
research.desc: Crop and livestock production x1.25 per level

research.name: The Seed Drill
research.hook: Around 1701 Jethro Tull built a horse-drawn seed drill that sowed seed in straight rows instead of scattering it by hand.

research.name: Diversified Farms
research.hook: By 1766 George Washington had given up tobacco at Mount Vernon for wheat, and later milled his own flour for market.
research.desc: Grain, hemp, horse and hide production x2

research.name: Society for Promoting Agriculture
research.hook: The Philadelphia Society for Promoting Agriculture, founded in 1785, offered premiums for farm experiments and reports.
research.desc: Colonists in farm colonies give +175% instead of +100%

research.name: Mouldboard of Least Resistance
research.hook: In 1794 Jefferson worked out a 'mouldboard of least resistance' for the plough and later described it to the Philosophical Society.

research.name: Improved Seed Stock
research.hook: From 1786 George Washington traded letters, seed and farming advice with the English agriculturist Arthur Young.
research.desc: Crop and livestock production x1.2 per level

research.name: Bartram's Garden
research.hook: John Bartram planted his garden beside the Schuylkill in 1728; it is the oldest surviving botanic garden in North America.

research.name: Tobacco Inspection Act
research.hook: Virginia's Tobacco Inspection Act of 1730 sent every hogshead through public warehouses, where inspectors burned trash leaf.
research.desc: Tobacco, cured tobacco and cigars sell x2

research.name: Carolina Indigo
research.hook: Eliza Lucas, running her family's South Carolina plantations from age 16, proved indigo as a crop there in the early 1740s.

research.name: Aboiteaux
research.hook: From the mid-1600s Acadian farmers on the Bay of Fundy diked the salt marshes, draining them through hinged sluices called aboiteaux.
research.desc: Marsh crops (indigo, hemp, sugar cane) production x3

research.name: The Cotton Gin
research.hook: Eli Whitney's gin of 1793 stripped seed from short-staple cotton at speed; it also deepened the South's reliance on slavery.

research.name: Selective Breeding
research.hook: From 1760 Robert Bakewell of Dishley, Leicestershire, bred sheep, cattle and heavy horses to a plan, keeping careful records.

research.name: Mission Ranchos
research.hook: Spanish missions in Texas and, from 1769, in California grazed great herds of cattle and horses on the open range.

research.name: The Narragansett Pacer
research.hook: Rhode Island's Narragansett Pacer, a smooth-gaited saddle horse, was prized in the 1700s from New England to the West Indies.
research.desc: Horses, leather and saddles sell x2

research.name: Royal Gift
research.hook: In 1785 Charles III of Spain sent George Washington a prize jack donkey, Royal Gift; Mount Vernon's mules followed.
research.desc: Colonists in horse and hide colonies give +250% instead of +100%

research.name: Water Sawmills
research.hook: One of the first sawmills in the colonies turned on the Great Works River at Berwick, Maine, in the 1630s.

research.name: Improved Felling
research.hook: Over the 1700s colonial smiths gave the felling axe a heavy poll for balance, making the 'American axe'.
research.desc: Timber, furs, ore and silver production x1.25 per level

research.name: Saugus Iron Works
research.hook: Around 1646 the Company of Undertakers began smelting iron at Hammersmith, now Saugus, Massachusetts.
research.desc: Charcoal Kiln and Blast Furnace work x2 faster

research.name: Cornwall Ore Banks
research.hook: Peter Grubb began working the Cornwall ore banks in Pennsylvania in the 1730s; the mine ran until 1973.

research.name: The Iron Act
research.hook: The Iron Act of 1750 let colonial pig and bar iron into Britain duty-free, but banned new slitting mills and steel furnaces.
research.desc: Pig iron and tools sell x2.5

research.name: The Schuyler Engine
research.hook: In 1755 Josiah Hornblower set a Newcomen engine pumping the Schuyler copper mine in New Jersey, the first steam engine in North America.
research.desc: Iron ore and silver production x3

research.name: Improved Smelting
research.hook: Henry William Stiegel took over Lancaster County's Elizabeth Furnace in 1757, rebuilt it, and cast iron stoves there; some survive today.
research.desc: Charcoal Kiln, Blast Furnace and Blacksmith x1.2 faster per level

research.name: Hopewell Furnace
research.hook: Mark Bird founded Hopewell Furnace in Pennsylvania in 1771; during the Revolution it cast cannon and shot for the Continental Army.
research.desc: Timber, furs, iron ore and silver production x3

research.name: The Wind Sawmill
research.hook: Cornelis Corneliszoon patented a wind-driven sawmill in Holland in 1593 and built one in 1594; the Dutch later carried sawmills to New Netherland.

research.name: Naval Stores Act
research.hook: The Naval Stores Act of 1705 paid bounties on colonial tar, pitch, turpentine, hemp and masts for the Royal Navy.

research.name: The King's Broad Arrow
research.hook: The 1691 Massachusetts charter reserved the great white pines for Royal Navy masts; surveyors blazed them with a broad arrow.
research.desc: Timber, lumber and tar sell x2.5

research.name: Live Oak Frames
research.hook: The frames of the frigate Constitution were cut from live oak on St. Simons Island, Georgia, in the mid-1790s.

research.name: Hudson's Bay Company
research.hook: Chartered in 1670, the Hudson's Bay Company traded cloth, kettles and tools to Cree and other hunters for beaver pelts.

research.name: Fort Orange
research.hook: From the Dutch post of Fort Orange, founded in 1624, Albany grew into the fur-trading heart of New York.

research.name: Grand Portage
research.hook: Montreal's North West Company, formed in 1779, met its canoe brigades each summer at Grand Portage on Lake Superior.
research.desc: Furs and fur coats sell x3

research.name: The Patio Process
research.hook: At Pachuca in 1554 Bartolome de Medina's patio process used mercury to draw silver from ore, powering New Spain's mines.

research.name: The Mexico City Mint
research.hook: The Mexico City mint, founded in 1535, was the first in the Americas; its silver dollars became the colonies' everyday coin.

research.name: La Valenciana
research.hook: Guanajuato's La Valenciana mine, opened in the 1760s, was by the 1790s among the richest silver mines in the world.

research.name: The Schooner
research.hook: Tradition says Andrew Robinson of Gloucester launched the first schooner in 1713; the handy fore-and-aft rig spread along the coast.

research.name: Improved Rigging
research.hook: Ropewalks, long sheds where hemp was walked and twisted into cordage, lined Boston's waterfront through the 1700s.
research.desc: Ships sail x1.2 faster per level

research.name: The Reflecting Quadrant
research.hook: Thomas Godfrey of Philadelphia and John Hadley of London each devised a reflecting quadrant around 1730-31.

research.name: Copper Sheathing
research.hook: HMS Alarm was sheathed in copper in 1761 as a trial; the clean hull kept off shipworm and weed and sailed faster.

research.name: American-Built Hulls
research.hook: By the 1770s perhaps a third of Britain's merchant ships had been built in American yards, of plentiful oak and pine.

research.name: The Lighthouse Act
research.hook: The ninth act of the first Congress, in August 1789, put the nation's lighthouses, beacons and buoys under federal care.

research.name: Improved Hulls
research.hook: Joshua Humphreys designed the long, stoutly built frigates ordered under the Naval Act of 1794, among them Constitution.
research.desc: Ships carry x1.2 cargo per level

research.name: The China Trade
research.hook: The Empress of China sailed from New York in February 1784, the first American ship to trade at Canton.
research.desc: Colonies on sea routes produce x3

research.name: The Grand Banks
research.hook: In the mid-1700s Marblehead was among the busiest fishing ports in the colonies, sending its schooners to the Grand Banks.

research.name: Nantucket Whaling
research.hook: From the 1710s Nantucket whalers hunted sperm whales in deep water; by the 1760s they boiled oil in try-works on deck.

research.name: Spermaceti Chandlers
research.hook: In 1761 chandlers of Newport, Providence, Boston and Philadelphia formed the United Company of Spermaceti Chandlers to cap the price of head matter.
research.desc: Whale oil and candles sell x2.5

research.name: Fishing Rights
research.hook: John Adams insisted on, and won in the 1783 Treaty of Paris, American fishing rights on the Grand Banks.
research.desc: Colonies on sea routes produce x2

research.name: Boston Light
research.hook: Boston Light on Little Brewster Island, first lit in September 1716, was the first lighthouse in the British colonies.

research.name: Chart of the Gulf Stream
research.hook: Franklin and his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket captain, charted the Gulf Stream; the chart was printed around 1769-70.

research.name: The Atlantic Neptune
research.hook: J.F.W. Des Barres's Atlantic Neptune, charts made for the Admiralty in the 1770s and 80s, mapped the coast in rich detail.

research.name: Letters of Marque
research.hook: From 1776 Congress licensed privateers; armed merchant ships took hundreds of British prizes during the war.

research.name: The Golden Rock
research.hook: Dutch St. Eustatius, the 'Golden Rock', traded with all sides; in 1776 its fort returned the salute of an American ship.

research.name: The Grand Turk
research.hook: Elias Hasket Derby's ship Grand Turk reached Canton in 1786, opening Salem's rich East India trade.

research.name: The Boston Post Road
research.hook: The first post rider left New York for Boston in January 1673, along the route that became the Boston Post Road.

research.name: Improved Teams
research.hook: The heavy Conestoga horse of Lancaster County pulled freight wagons in teams of four to six through the 1700s.
research.desc: Wagons carry x1.25 cargo per level

research.name: The Great Wagon Road
research.hook: From the 1740s settlers took the Great Wagon Road from Philadelphia down the Shenandoah Valley to the Carolina backcountry.

research.name: The Conestoga Wagon
research.hook: Built in Pennsylvania's Conestoga valley by the mid-1700s, the wagon's boat-shaped bed kept loads from shifting on hills.

research.name: Postmaster Franklin
research.hook: Made joint deputy postmaster general for the colonies in 1753, Franklin surveyed the post roads, sped the mails and made the post pay.

research.name: The Lancaster Turnpike
research.hook: The Lancaster Turnpike, chartered in 1792 and finished in 1795, was America's first long stone-surfaced toll road.

research.name: Improved Roadbeds
research.hook: Where roads crossed swamp and mud, colonists laid logs side by side to make 'corduroy' roads a loaded wagon could cross.
research.desc: Wagons travel x1.2 faster per level

research.name: The Wilderness Road
research.hook: In 1775 Daniel Boone and some thirty axemen marked the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap into Kentucky.
research.desc: Colonies on land routes produce x3

research.name: The Pennypack Bridge
research.hook: The stone bridge over Pennypack Creek, built in 1697 at William Penn's urging, still carries traffic in Philadelphia.

research.name: The Durham Boat
research.hook: Long, shallow Durham boats, named for Pennsylvania's Durham iron country and in use by the mid-1700s, carried iron and grain down the Delaware.

research.name: The Potomac Company
research.hook: Washington's Potomac Company, chartered in 1785, cleared the river and cut skirting canals around its falls.

research.name: Ohio Flatboats
research.hook: In the late 1780s and 1790s thousands of settlers floated down the Ohio from Pittsburgh on flatboats.

research.name: The Cumberland Gap
research.hook: In 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker of the Loyal Land Company passed through the Cumberland Gap and named it.
research.desc: Scouts reveal x1.5 more of the map

research.name: Mason and Dixon's Line
research.hook: Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon surveyed the boundary between Pennsylvania and Maryland from 1763 to 1767.

research.name: Rittenhouse's Lines
research.hook: In the 1780s David Rittenhouse helped run Pennsylvania's boundary lines, sighting with instruments he had made himself.

research.name: The Land Ordinance
research.hook: The Land Ordinance of 1785 laid out western lands in six-mile-square townships; Thomas Hutchins led the first survey.

research.name: Apprenticeships
research.hook: In 1718 twelve-year-old Benjamin Franklin was bound apprentice to his brother James, a Boston printer.

research.name: Improved Benches
research.hook: Philadelphia's master builders founded the Carpenters' Company in 1724 and kept a book of prices for their work.
research.desc: All workshops x1.2 faster per level

research.name: The Library Company
research.hook: Franklin and his Junto founded the Library Company of Philadelphia in 1731 so tradesmen could share costly books.

research.name: Bethlehem Waterworks
research.hook: In 1754 the Moravians of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, pumped spring water uphill by waterwheel: the colonies' first public waterworks.

research.name: Report on Manufactures
research.hook: Hamilton's Report on Manufactures, sent to Congress in December 1791, urged bounties and support for American industry.

research.name: Slater Mill
research.hook: Samuel Slater, who carried Arkwright's machines in his memory, built Slater Mill at Pawtucket, Rhode Island, in 1793.
research.desc: Every staffed workshop counts 1 extra colonist

research.name: Improved Wares
research.hook: Under the Patent Act of 1790, Samuel Hopkins received the first U.S. patent, for a better way of making potash.
research.desc: Crafted goods sell x1.15 per level

research.name: Society for Useful Manufactures
research.hook: Hamilton's Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, chartered in 1791, founded Paterson, New Jersey, at the Great Falls.

research.name: The Flying Shuttle
research.hook: John Kay's flying shuttle, patented in 1733, let one weaver send the shuttle across a broad loom.

research.name: The Spinning Jenny
research.hook: James Hargreaves built his spinning jenny in Lancashire around 1764; one worker could spin eight threads at once.

research.name: Homespun
research.hook: During the boycotts of 1768-69 'Daughters of Liberty' held spinning bees to make homespun in place of British cloth.
research.desc: Dyed cloth needs 1 cloth instead of 2

research.name: Beverly Cotton Manufactory
research.hook: The Beverly Cotton Manufactory in Massachusetts, begun in 1787, was among America's first cotton mills; Washington toured it in 1789.
research.desc: Weaver's House, Sail Loft, Dye House and Tailor x3 faster

research.name: The Pennsylvania Rifle
research.hook: By the 1740s German-born gunsmiths in Lancaster County were rifling long hunting guns: the Pennsylvania rifle.

research.name: Interchangeable Parts
research.hook: In 1785 Jefferson visited Honore Blanc in France, whose musket locks were made from parts that fit any lock.
research.desc: Muskets need 1 pig iron instead of 2

research.name: Revere's Foundry
research.hook: In 1788 Paul Revere opened a foundry in Boston's North End, casting iron and brass and, later, church bells.
research.desc: Blacksmith, Cooperage and Silversmith x2.5 faster

research.name: Springfield Armory
research.hook: Springfield, Massachusetts, a Continental arsenal from 1777, began making its own muskets in 1795.
research.desc: Armory, Saddlery and Cavalry Barracks x3 faster

research.name: Faneuil Hall
research.hook: Peter Faneuil gave Boston a market hall in 1742, with a meeting room upstairs where the town meeting gathered.

research.name: Improved Trade
research.hook: Franklin's 'The Way to Wealth' (1758) gathered Poor Richard's sayings on thrift and industry into one speech.
research.desc: All goods sell x1.1 per level

research.name: The Pennsylvania Gazette
research.hook: Franklin bought the Pennsylvania Gazette in 1729 and filled it with news, essays and merchants' advertisements.

research.name: The London Coffee House
research.hook: Printer William Bradford opened the London Coffee House in Philadelphia in 1754; merchants met there daily to trade.
research.desc: Goods in glut sell at x0.8 instead of x0.6

research.name: The Buttonwood Agreement
research.hook: In May 1792 twenty-four New York brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement, the root of the New York Stock Exchange.
research.desc: Wanted goods sell at x2 instead of x1.6

research.name: Bank of North America
research.hook: Chartered by Congress in 1781 and opened in January 1782, Robert Morris's Bank of North America was the nation's first chartered bank.

research.name: Improved Statecraft
research.hook: Pennsylvania's State House, built 1732-1753, housed the colonial assembly and later the Continental Congress.
research.desc: Liberty at independence x1.1 per level

research.name: The Continental Congress
research.hook: The First Continental Congress met at Carpenters' Hall, Philadelphia, in September 1774, with delegates from twelve colonies.

research.name: The Albany Plan
research.hook: At Albany in 1754 Franklin proposed a union of the colonies under a grand council; no colony adopted it.

research.name: The Stamp Act Congress
research.hook: In October 1765 delegates from nine colonies met in New York to protest the Stamp Act.

research.name: The Olive Branch Petition
research.hook: In July 1775 Congress sent the king John Dickinson's Olive Branch Petition; George III refused to receive it.
research.desc: Royal Favor lasts twice as long

research.name: Non-Importation
research.hook: In 1768 Boston merchants agreed to stop importing British goods; other ports followed, until the boycott collapsed in 1770.

research.name: Bills of Credit
research.hook: In 1690 Massachusetts issued paper bills of credit, among the first government paper money in the Western world.

research.name: The Contributionship
research.hook: Franklin helped found the Philadelphia Contributionship in 1752, the colonies' first successful fire insurance company.
research.desc: Colonies keep working 1 more hour while you are away

research.name: The Mint
research.hook: The Coinage Act of 1792 founded the U.S. Mint in Philadelphia, with David Rittenhouse as its first director.

research.name: Committees of Correspondence
research.hook: Boston formed a Committee of Correspondence in 1772 at Samuel Adams's urging; soon the colonies were writing to one another.

research.name: The Goddard Broadside
research.hook: In January 1777 Congress had Mary Katherine Goddard of Baltimore print the Declaration with the signers' names.

research.name: Peale's Museum
research.hook: Charles Willson Peale opened his museum of portraits and natural history in Philadelphia in 1786.
